# Project Overview

The goal of this project is to explore sentiment analysis
using R and Tidyverse. I will reproduce the sentiment
analysis presented in Chapter 2 of the book "Text Mining
with R" by Julia Silge and David Robinson.

To extend the original analysis, I will use a different
text dataset related to electric vehicle reviews and
include an additional sentiment lexicon.

As an electrical engineer, I am interested in understanding
how people describe electric vehicle performance, battery
life, driving range, and charging systems.

This project will help me understand how different sentiment
lexicons can influence the results of text analysis.

# Research Questions

1. What are the most common positive and negative words
   in electric vehicle reviews?

2. What is the overall sentiment of electric vehicle reviews?

3. How do sentiment analysis results vary across different
   sentiment lexicons?

4. How do the results from the electric vehicle dataset
   differ from the original Chapter 2 analysis?
   
# Data Source

The dataset selected for this project is the Expert Review
Dataset on Electric Quadricycles, available on Zenodo.

The dataset contains 95 reviews of small electric vehicles.
The original data includes three variables:

- Brand: Electric vehicle brand or model.
- URL: Original source of the review.
- Text: Full text of the vehicle review.

The Excel file contains five sheets. For this project,
I will use only the "Original data" sheet because I want
to perform my own sentiment analysis using R.

**Source:** https://zenodo.org/records/14501242

## Data Import

```{r data-import}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Import the original dataset
ev_reviews <- read_excel(
  "Data/Data Notes - Dataset.xlsx",
  sheet = "Original data"
)
```

The original dataset was imported from an Excel file.
The following tables show the dataset dimensions,
variable descriptions, and a preview of the data.

## Dataset Overview


# Data Validation

Before performing sentiment analysis, I will check the
quality of the dataset. This includes checking for missing
values, duplicate records, and empty review texts.

## Missing Values

```{r missing-values}
# Check missing values by variable
missing_summary <- tibble(
  Variable = names(ev_reviews),
  `Missing Values` = colSums(is.na(ev_reviews)),
  Percentage = round(
    colMeans(is.na(ev_reviews)) * 100, 2
  )
)

missing_summary %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Table 4. Missing Values",
    align = c("l", "c", "c")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
```

## Reviews by Vehicle

```{r reviews-by-vehicle}
# Count reviews by vehicle brand or model
vehicle_summary <- ev_reviews %>%
  count(Brand, name = "Reviews", sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = round(Reviews / sum(Reviews) * 100, 2)
  )

vehicle_summary %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Table 5. Number of Reviews by Vehicle",
    align = c("l", "c", "c")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The number of reviews may vary across vehicles.
This is important to consider when comparing
sentiment analysis results.

# Original Analysis and Proposed Extension

## Original Analysis

The original analysis is based on Chapter 2 of the book
"Text Mining with R" by Julia Silge and David Robinson.

The authors use Jane Austen's books to demonstrate how
sentiment analysis works with tidy data. They use three
sentiment lexicons: AFINN, Bing, and NRC.

I will reproduce the original analysis to understand how
these methods work.

## Proposed Extension

To extend the original analysis, I will use a different
dataset containing 95 electric vehicle reviews.

I will also include the Loughran-McDonald lexicon as an
additional sentiment lexicon.

This extension will allow me to compare sentiment results
using different types of text and sentiment lexicons.

# Methodology

The analysis will be developed in R using Tidyverse
and tidytext.

The following steps will be used:

1. Reproduce the original sentiment analysis from Chapter 2.
2. Import and validate the electric vehicle dataset.
3. Clean and prepare the text data.
4. Convert the text into individual words using tokenization.
5. Remove common words when appropriate.
6. Apply the AFINN, Bing, NRC, and Loughran-McDonald lexicons.
7. Compare sentiment results across vehicle brands and models.
8. Create visualizations using ggplot2.
9. Compare the results and explain the main findings.

## Sentiment Lexicons

```{r sentiment-lexicons}
lexicon_summary <- tibble(
  Lexicon = c(
    "AFINN",
    "Bing",
    "NRC",
    "Loughran-McDonald"
  ),
  Description = c(
    "Uses numerical sentiment scores from -5 to 5",
    "Classifies words as positive or negative",
    "Classifies words by sentiment and emotion",
    "Classifies words using financial sentiment categories"
  ),
  Purpose = c(
    "Original analysis",
    "Original analysis",
    "Original analysis",
    "Proposed extension"
  )
)

lexicon_summary %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Table 6. Sentiment Lexicons",
    align = "l"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = TRUE,
    position = "center"
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

Each lexicon uses a different method to score and classify words. For this reason, I will use normalized values to make the sentiment scores comparable.

# Expected Results

I expect to identify common positive and negative words
in electric vehicle reviews.

I also expect to find different sentiment patterns
across vehicle brands and models.

The comparison between the four sentiment lexicons
may show how different methods can produce different
results using the same text.

# Limitations

This project has some limitations:

- The dataset contains only 95 reviews.
- The number of reviews may vary across vehicles.
- The sentiment lexicons may not recognize some
  technical electrical and automotive terms.
- Sentiment analysis may not correctly identify
  sarcasm, negation, or the meaning of words
  in specific contexts.
- The Loughran-McDonald lexicon was designed for
  financial text, which may affect its results.

These limitations will be considered when interpreting
the final results.
